PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT

MEMORANDUM

TO: Engagement Team and Deal Committee
FROM: Arbitration & International Dispute Resolution Group
DATE: August 10, 2026
RE: Analysis of Counterparty Markup of Arbitration Agreement — Recommendations for Accept/Reject/Counter Positions

I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

We have completed our review of the counterparty's redline markup against the original draft arbitration agreement, the SPA excerpts, and the internal deal-team playbook. The counterparty's revision accepts most firm-standard provisions but introduces four categories of deviations that must be addressed: (1) an indemnification cap change with the basket converted from a deductible to a tipping mechanism; (2) a Material Adverse Effect (MAE) definition that adds carve-outs for regulatory action of exactly the kind disclosed on Schedule 3.7; (3) a new limitation period that shortens survival for core representations; and (4) a new special indemnity for disclosed matters. Each deviation is analyzed below against the original base materials, the SPA terms, our internal playbook, and the client's controlling instructions.

Consistent with the latest partner direction on this engagement, we treat the basket conversion as a conceded point (client will not contest it), but any survival-period reduction is treated as a walk-away issue. Our counter-positions and recommended negotiation strategy are set out in Section VIII.

II. SOURCE MATERIALS REVIEWED

The following materials were reviewed in connection with this analysis:

1. Matter File — Arbitration International Dispute Resolution (Matter File 2)
2. Counterparty Markup — identifying deviations from firm-standard provisions
3. Schedules and Exhibits — including Schedule 3.7 (pending regulatory inquiries), Schedule 5.2 (retained liabilities), and Exhibit B (survival matrix)
4. Deal Team Correspondence — partner email thread establishing controlling negotiation priorities
5. Deep-Drafting Pack — including the underlying transaction agreement (Share Purchase Agreement), the counterparty's second-turn markup, the internal approved indemnity positions memo (privileged), and the relevant disclosure schedules
6. Northgale Commercial Contracting Playbook (2026 Edition) — for applicable standards on commercial contracting matters
7. Clause Library — including unapproved counterparty-supplied governing law language (CL-090)
8. Arbitration Clause Review Memorandum — institutional rules mapping (ICC, LCIA, SIAC, UNCITRAL)

The scheduled exceptions in the disclosure schedules control over general statements in the base materials. Where the deal correspondence updates or supersedes earlier positions, only the latest controlling instruction governs.

III. TRANSACTION AND ARBITRATION FRAMEWORK

The engagement concerns a transaction structured through a Share Purchase Agreement (SPA) in which our client, the seller, has provided certain representations, warranties, and indemnification obligations to the buyer. The transaction documentation includes an arbitration agreement (or dispute resolution framework) providing for resolution of disputes through international commercial arbitration. The counterparty has returned a redline markup affecting the core commercial terms of the deal.

The operative transaction documents establish the following baseline parameters:

• Purchase Price: $120,000,000
• General representations survival: eighteen (18) months
• Fundamental representations survival: six (6) years
• Tax representations survival: until 60 days after expiration of applicable statute of limitations
• Indemnification deductible: $400,000 (true deductible — recovery only in excess of deductible)
• Indemnification cap: 10% of Purchase Price ($12,000,000), with Fundamental Representations capped at the full Purchase Price
• Materiality scrape: materiality qualifiers disregarded for purposes of calculating Losses
• Exclusive remedy: Article VIII is sole and exclusive post-Closing remedy, other than fraud and equitable claims
• Order of recovery: Buyer recovers first from Escrow Amount, then severally from Sellers

The counterparty's markup introduces changes to these baseline terms, as well as new provisions requiring analysis.

IV. COUNTERPARTY MARKUP — DEVIATIONS IDENTIFIED

A. Indemnification Cap and Basket

Counterparty Proposal. The counterparty's markup makes changes to the indemnification mechanics:

1. Basket Conversion. The original $400,000 true deductible (recovery only for amounts in excess of the deductible) is converted to a $250,000 tipping basket. Under the counterproposal, once aggregate Losses exceed $250,000, the Sellers are liable from the first dollar. This structurally increases Seller exposure: for claims above $250,000 but below $400,000, Seller now bears liability it previously avoided entirely; for claims above $400,000, Seller now bears the first $400,000 that previously fell outside its liability exposure.

2. Cap Change. The marked-up cap is stated in modified terms relative to the base draft. Under the base draft, the Sellers' aggregate liability under Section 8.2(a) is capped at ten percent (10%) of the Purchase Price ($12,000,000). The counterparty's revision modifies this cap, and the modification must be evaluated against the internal playbook's approved fallback floor.

B. Material Adverse Effect (MAE) Definition — New Regulatory Carve-Outs

Counterparty Proposal. The counterparty's markup amends the definition of "Material Adverse Effect" to add carve-outs for regulatory action. The new carve-outs extend to "regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this matter," meaning actions of the nature disclosed on the disclosure schedules. On the face of the markup, the carve-out language is broader than the pending regulatory matters disclosed on Schedule 3.7, and would appear to exclude from the MAE definition any adverse effect attributable to regulatory action — including future regulatory action not disclosed at signing or closing.

Analysis. Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries. The regulatory carve-outs in the MAE definition, as drafted by the counterparty, would narrow the scope of what constitutes an MAE that permits the buyer to decline to close or reduces the seller's exposure for regulatory-driven losses. From the seller's perspective, however, a broader MAE carve-out is favorable because it reduces the buyer's ability to avoid closing based on regulatory developments. The key drafting concern is whether the carve-out language inadvertently creates unintended consequences, such as foreclosing seller protections.

C. Survival Period — Limitation Period Change

Counterparty Proposal. The counterparty's markup introduces a new limitation period that shortens the survival period for core representations. The original draft provides for an eighteen (18) month survival period for general representations and warranties. The counterparty's revision shortens this period, which materially affects the seller's indemnification exposure and the buyer's ability to assert post-closing claims.

Analysis. Per the controlling deal correspondence, our client "treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue." This is consistent with the internal playbook, which sets the approved fallback at a maximum of twenty-four (24) months and treats a thirty-six (36) month survival period as out of policy. More critically, any reduction below the eighteen (18) month baseline would be unacceptable as a matter of the client's stated position.

The interaction between the survival period and the disclosure schedules is material. Exhibit B sets the survival matrix for the various representation categories. The counterparty's limitation-period change contradicts the Exhibit B matrix. Per the schedules document: "Exhibit B sets the survival matrix the markup's limitation-period change contradicts."

D. New Special Indemnity for Disclosed Matters

Counterparty Proposal. The counterparty's markup adds a new provision: the Sellers shall indemnify Buyer for any and all Losses arising out of or relating to the matters disclosed on the relevant schedule (Schedule 3.14). The new special indemnity:
• Is NOT subject to the Deductible or the cap in Section 8.3
• Survives until the expiration of the applicable statutes of limitation
• Is recoverable directly from the Sellers without first exhausting the Escrow Amount (per a conforming change to the order-of-recovery provision)

Analysis. The new special indemnity is materially overbroad in at least four respects:

1. Scope. The special indemnity extends to "any and all Losses arising out of or relating to the matters disclosed on Schedule 3.14," without distinguishing between the separately-described items on that schedule. Per the playbook (IP-4), any acceptable special indemnity must be limited in scope to Schedule 3.14 Item 1 (pending TTAB opposition) and Item 2 (pending customer dispute), with resolved matters (e.g., the OSHA citation at Item 3) expressly excluded.

2. Cap. The special indemnity carries no cap. Per the playbook (IP-4), any acceptable special indemnity must have an aggregate cap of $2,500,000. An uncapped special indemnity is out of policy.

3. Survival. The special indemnity survives until "the expiration of the applicable statutes of limitation." Per the playbook (IP-4), any acceptable special indemnity must have a survival period of twenty-four (24) months from Closing. Indefinite or limitations-based survival is out of policy.

4. Order of Recovery. The conforming change to the order-of-recovery provision provides that special-indemnity claims are recoverable directly from the Sellers without first exhausting the Escrow Amount. This deprives the Sellers of the benefit of the escrow mechanism and should be rejected.

E. Counterparty-Supplied Governing Law — Clause Library Reference

The clause library contains an unapproved counterparty-supplied governing law provision (CL-090) providing for "the laws of the Cayman Islands and disputes... resolved by ad hoc arbitration seated in a jurisdiction to be agreed." This language is not firm precedent, has not been approved by the Contracts KM Committee, and should not be adopted. Ad hoc arbitration under an unascertained seat ("a jurisdiction to be agreed") presents material risks of non-enforceability and should be rejected if proposed.

F. Arbitration Rules and Seating

The arbitration framework in the transaction should follow established institutional rules rather than ad hoc arbitration. Based on the firm's arbitration clause review memorandum, the firm recognizes four classifications:

• ICC Rules of Arbitration — ICC Administered
• LCIA Arbitration Rules — LCIA Administered
• SIAC Arbitration Rules — SIAC Administered
• UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules — ad hoc (unless separately appointing an institution)

Any arbitration agreement that names a specific set of institutional rules should be classified by the rules it adopts, not by the hearing venue city. Where the counterparty has proposed ad hoc arbitration or ambiguous case administration, such provisions should be rejected as uncertain and potentially unenforceable.

V. RECONCILIATION WITH SCHEDULES AND EXHIBITS

A. Schedule 3.7 — Pending Regulatory Inquiries

Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries. These inquiries intersect directly with the counterparty's proposed MAE carve-outs for regulatory action. Any MAE carve-out language must be carefully drafted to avoid creating an exception that would swallow the MAE definition entirely. The scheduled exceptions in the disclosure schedules control over general statements in the base materials.

B. Schedule 5.2 — Retained Liabilities

Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities. The markup's indemnification changes would silently shift these liabilities to the Sellers through the cap reduction, basket conversion, and special indemnity provisions. The deliverable must reconcile both sources against the base materials.

C. Exhibit B — Survival Matrix

Exhibit B sets the survival matrix for the transaction. The counterparty's limitation-period change contradicts the survival matrix in Exhibit B. The scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials.

VI. CONTROLLING PARTNER DIRECTIONS FROM DEAL CORRESPONDENCE

The deal correspondence contains a partner email thread on this engagement. Critically, the latest message REVISES the analysis priorities:

• The client will concede the basket conversion.
• The client treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue.

Earlier messages in the thread state the opposite priority ordering; only the latest message controls. The deliverable must reflect the controlling instruction, not the superseded one.

This controlling direction has significant implications for our negotiation strategy:

• Since the client will concede the basket conversion, we should not expend negotiation capital on this issue, and we should accept the $250,000 tipping basket as proposed (subject to confirming that the proposed threshold is at or above our acceptable floor when expressed on an equivalent basis).
• Since survival-period reduction is a walk-away issue for the client, any attempt by the counterparty to reduce survival below the established baseline should be met with a firm and non-negotiable position.

VII. PLAYBOOK POSITIONS (INTERNAL APPROVED INDEMNITY STANDARDS)

Our internal playbook (Trellis deal team approved indemnity positions, approved by the Transaction Committee on 24 July 2026) establishes the following standards:

• IP-1 (Survival — general representations): Opening 18 months; fallback 24 months; 36 months out of policy.
• IP-2 (Indemnity cap): Opening 10% of Purchase Price ($12,000,000); fallback 15% ($18,000,000); 25% out of policy.
• IP-3 (Basket): Must remain a true deductible; conversion to a tipping basket is out of policy at any threshold. Deductible may be reduced from $400,000 but not below a floor of $300,000.
• IP-4 (Special indemnity): Acceptable only if all of the following hold: (i) scope limited to Schedule 3.14 Item 1 and Item 2 (pending matters); (ii) aggregate cap of $2,500,000; (iii) survival of 24 months from Closing; and (iv) resolved matters (including Schedule 3.14 Item 3) expressly excluded. An uncapped special indemnity, or one extending to resolved matters, is out of policy.
• IP-5 (Logistics): All Project Lattice work product filed under Trellis naming conventions; no adoption of counterparty-proposed filenames or transmittal logistics for internal workspace. Counterparty logistics apply only to what we send them, after sign-off.

Quantification note: Escalation analyses must state cap deltas in dollars against the $120,000,000 Purchase Price and identify which asks exceed the deal team's delegated authority.

VIII. RECOMMENDATIONS — ACCEPT / REJECT / COUNTER

A. Basket Conversion (Counterparty's Tipping Basket)

Recommendation: ACCEPT (per controlling partner direction).

The client's latest instruction concedes the basket conversion. Although our playbook treats any tipping basket as out of policy (IP-3), the client has determined that this point is not worth pursuing. We recommend accepting the $250,000 tipping basket as proposed, subject to confirming that the proposed threshold of $250,000 is at or above our $300,000 deductible floor when expressed on an equivalent basis. If the proposed threshold would result in Sellers bearing liability at a level below the $300,000 floor, we may need to negotiate the threshold upward even while conceding the conversion mechanism.

B. Indemnification Cap

Recommendation: REJECT / COUNTER.

The counterparty's cap modification must be evaluated against the playbook's parameters:
• Opening position: 10% of Purchase Price ($12,000,000)
• Approved fallback: maximum 15% of Purchase Price ($18,000,000)
• Out of policy: Any cap above 15%

If the counterparty's markup changes the cap in a manner that reduces seller protection, we should counter at our approved fallback of 15% to maintain sufficient protection. Any cap above 15% requires escalation to Special Committee.

Quantification: A cap at 15% would set Seller exposure at $18,000,000 (delta of $6,000,000 above the standard position). A cap at 25% would set Seller exposure at $30,000,000 (delta of $18,000,000 above the standard position). Any cap above 15% is out of policy and requires escalation.

C. MAE Definition — Regulatory Carve-Outs

Recommendation: REJECT IN PART / COUNTER.

The MAE carve-out for regulatory action, as drafted, is overbroad and would cover future regulatory action not disclosed at signing. We should counter with language that limits the carve-out to:
1. Changes in law or regulation generally applicable to the industry (not Company-specific)
2. Regulatory actions disclosed on Schedule 3.7 as of the signing date
3. Any other regulatory action that does not individually or in the aggregate have a material adverse effect on the Company

The carve-out should not extend to regulatory actions that arise from the Company's own acts or omissions that were known or reasonably foreseeable at signing and were not disclosed on the schedules.

D. Survival Period

Recommendation: REJECT (WALK-AWAY ISSUE).

Per the controlling partner instruction, any survival-period reduction is a walk-away issue for the client. We should not make any concession on this point. If the counterparty insists on a shortened survival period, we should escalate to the client before continuing negotiations.

If the counterparty attempts to shorten the eighteen (18) month general representation survival period, we will reject the change in full. If the counterparty is seeking an increase in survival (i.e., from 18 to 36 months as in a related matter), our playbook limits acceptability to 24 months maximum, with 36 months being out of policy.

E. New Special Indemnity

Recommendation: REJECT AS DRAFTED / COUNTER.

The special indemnity as proposed is not acceptable. We counter with the following parameters per IP-4:

1. Scope: Limited to Schedule 3.14 Item 1 (Trademark opposition) and Item 2 (Customer dispute). Schedule 3.14 Item 3 (OSHA citation — resolved) is expressly excluded.
2. Cap: Aggregate cap of $2,500,000.
3. Survival: Twenty-four (24) months from Closing.
4. Subject to basket and cap: The special indemnity should be subject to the basket and cap provisions of Section 8.3.
5. Order of Recovery: Special-indemnity claims should follow the same order of recovery as other indemnity claims (i.e., first from Escrow Amount, then severally from Sellers). We should reject the counterparty's conforming change to the order-of-recovery provision.

F. Governing Law and Arbitration Framework

Recommendation: REJECT any counterparty-supplied governing law or ad hoc arbitration provisions that are not firm precedent.

The counterparty-supplied governing law language (Cayman Islands law, ad hoc arbitration, unfixed seat) is not approved and should not be adopted. If the counterparty proposes changing the governing law or arbitration rules, we should maintain our position consistent with the firm's arbitration clause review standards and institutional rules mapping.

G. Logistics

Recommendation: ACCEPT only with sign-off.

Per IP-5, we will not adopt counterparty-proposed filenames, data-room mirroring requests, or transmittal logistics for our internal workspace. Counterparty logistics apply only to what we send them, after sign-off.

IX. QUANTIFIED EXPOSURE ANALYSIS

For the escalation/approval materials, the following quantified exposure is relevant. All figures are based on the $120,000,000 Purchase Price.

A. Cap Delta
• Standard position (opening): $12,000,000 (10% of Purchase Price)
• Approved fallback: $18,000,000 (15% of Purchase Price)
• Out of policy (e.g., 25%): $30,000,000 (25% of Purchase Price)
• Delta from standard to fallback: $6,000,000
• Delta from standard to 25%: $18,000,000

B. Basket Conversion Impact
• True deductible ($400,000): Seller bears no liability until aggregate Losses exceed $400,000; recovery limited to excess
• Tipping basket ($250,000): Seller bears liability from first dollar once aggregate Losses exceed $250,000
• Exposure delta: (i) For claims in the range of $250,000-$400,000, Seller now bears full liability instead of none; (ii) For claims above $400,000, Seller bears an additional $400,000 that was previously excluded from protection

C. Survival Period Impact
• Reduction from 18 months to a shorter period would reduce the window for asserting claims and indemnification rights
• If the counterparty proposes a shorter period, this is a walk-away issue per the client's instruction

X. ESCALATION REQUIREMENTS

The following items require escalation beyond the deal team's delegated authority:

1. Any cap above 15% ($18,000,000) — requires Special Committee approval per IP-2
2. Any special indemnity that is uncapped, extends to resolved matters, or has survival beyond 24 months — requires Special Committee approval per IP-4
3. Any survival period change that reduces the general representation survival below 18 months — walk-away issue per controlling partner instruction; escalation to client required before any concession
4. Any change to the governing law or arbitration rules — requires Contracts KM Committee approval and review against firm precedent

XI. SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDED POSITIONS

The following table summarizes our recommended positions on each counterparty change:

1. BASKET: Converted from $400K true deductible to $250K tipping basket → ACCEPT (per client direction)
2. CAP: Modified from base 10% ($12M) → REJECT/COUNTER at approved fallback of 15% ($18M); any cap above 15% requires escalation
3. MAE: Regulatory carve-outs added → COUNTER — limit to disclosed matters and industry-wide changes
4. SURVIVAL: Shortened limitation period → REJECT (walk-away issue)
5. SPECIAL INDEMNITY: Uncapped, indefinite survival, direct recovery → REJECT AS DRAFTED / COUNTER per IP-4 parameters
6. GOVERNING LAW/ARBITRATION RULES: Counterparty-supplied → REJECT unless consistent with firm-approved precedent
7. LOGISTICS: → ACCEPT only with sign-off per IP-5

XII. NEXT STEPS

1. Prepare counter-redline responses to the counterparty reflecting the above positions
2. Escalate the survival-period issue and any cap above 15% to the client/Special Committee
3. Confirm the basket concession thresholds with the client and the deal team
4. Prepare the escalation/approval memorandum for any out-of-policy asks
5. Coordinate with the transaction team on the MAE carve-out counter-language
6. Engage with outside counsel on the arbitration rules framework to ensure the arbitration agreement provisions remain enforceable and consistent with firm precedent

This memorandum is prepared for internal negotiation purposes and is privileged and confidential. It should be handled in accordance with the firm's privilege protocols for transaction negotiations.

[END OF MEMORANDUM]
